doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
title: The decline of the clarinet's popularity
summary: He says every instrument has its day and he stuck with the clarinet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, and another thing that we should address is around this time, sort of towards the later fifties, the clarinet, which had been the king of instruments started to declined in popularity.
And no one can account for the public’s taste, and you can’t really control it.

Although, every instrument has it’s place in the sun from time to time. I could remember when the organ, electric organ, was a joke and the accordion was laughed at. And harmonica, my gosh, that was really a joke in jazz.

And then when you hear like guys like Toots Thielemans play, and who’s the young fellow in Chicago now who’s a . . . I played with him, do you remember his name? I can’t . . . Young fellow in Chicago I recently played with.

Jazz harmonica, terrific. So, there you go, you know. Every instrument will shine. Even the saxophone kind of dwindled at a certain period of time. But the clarinet dwindled longer than most. [laughter]
And could you feel that coming, you know, as that was beginning to happen?
Yeah, I could feel it and I knew it, but I was a clarinet player, sink or swim. So, I stayed with it.
Well you’d already sold your alto sax so what are you going to do?
